utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we take the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Stanisic Defence team, Slobodan Cvijetic, Tatjana Savic, and Eugene O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness comes in, and in order to save argument at a later stage, can I raise one matter relating to the evidence that I understand that he's going to give. Your Honours may have seen in the 65 ter statement for this witness -- first of all, I understand the length of examination-in-chief has gone up, for which I believe the Defence need your leave, from eight to ten hours. Second, according to the 65 ter summary, this witness is going to provide a detailed account, and I emphasise the word "detailed," of the situation in the SJB Novo Sarajevo prior to April 1992 and the attack on that SJB in April 1992. Your Honours, it is not within the realms of the indictment, this particular municipality or SJB, so at the moment we say it's objectionable to lead evidence on that because it isn't relevant. Your Honours, secondly, I've had a remarkable e-mail which alleges that it is a proofing note. It says that the witness will explain his role in drafting some of the RS MUP regulations, that's fine, and the planning of the Foca action. Now, Your Honours, two matters. Firstly, it is not good enough to talk about saying "planning of the Foca action" without explaining what on earth that means or what it is to cover. And secondly, Foca is also not a municipality in this indictment. So, Your Honours, at the moment, may I make it clear, I object to this evidence. As I say, rather than waiting for it to start, I thought it would be simpler to deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as the first objection is concerned, you know that we dealt with this situation in Sarajevo immediately before the outbreak of the war, and that is part of the general context of the events. The witness will link that with his departure from Sarajevo and the reasons for that departure. We have heard evidence on that already, and this witness is possibly the most competent to speak about it because he was a member of the police station which was immediately attacked and he was actually a victim, which also triggered some subsequent events. And these are also some reasons why the joint MUP stopped functioning. This is also a topic we dealt with, and it is also a prominent topic in the indictment. As far as the second objection is concerned, and it pertains to the contents of the witness's evidence, we did state in a proofing note that he would speak about his participation in the drafting of some regulations in the MUP. As for the planned Foca operation, it is part of the context of his evidence about field trips in the capacity of an inspector of the Crime Prevention and Combatting Administration, and the bulk of his testimony is about that. Among other field trips and visits, he will also mention the plans to take part in that operation. I also believe that the previous witness introduced this element that this witness who is about to testify was supposed to take part in the operation to arrest some persons. Among other SJBs, he visited Foca, Cajnice, and all the others that are contained in the indictment. In the context of these visits and field trips, he will mention Foca, but no more than that. You needn't worry, we will not unduly waste time on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is still -- firstly, my objection still stands. Secondly, he hasn't explained what he is talking about with the Foca operation. If this is what the witness is going to talk about and this is completely brand new evidence, we should have had a full account in the proofing note of what it was the witness was going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is labouring under a bit of a handicap in that we haven't yet seen the proofing note in respect of this witness. So in terms of the exchange between the Bench and counsel on each side, we aren't sure exactly to what extent Ms. Korner's complaint, for want of a better word, about being handicapped is -- how the -- the strength of that objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, it was sent to -- it's not a proofing note at all -- It's not a proofing note at all, it's an e-mail sent to Ms. Featherstone; Mr. Dygeus, who I don't believe is here; myself; Mr. Smith; Mr. Cvijetic, for some reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The same three-line summary or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It says: "Dear all, please be advised that MS-008 will also explain his role in drafting some of the RS MUP regulations," without explaining what that role was, which regulations. "And," and I'm reading, "planning of the 'Foca action.'" That's it. This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we are all on the same page in the same hymn-book, let me hear from Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And should I -- I should add this, Mr. Cvijetic will ask for ten hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, having regard to the purpose that a proofing note serves, both as notice to the side opposite and in terms of assisting the Chamber, isn't there a serious deficiency here?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I don't see a problem at all. We announced what the witness would speak about, and we are not supposed to submit his complete statement or interview. It is enough -- an outline is enough. The Prosecution knows what the witness is familiar with and about what from their contacts with him. We did not -- our motion was not that the witness should be a witness under a 92 ter. So he will speak about the same things that he spoke about to the OTP and the topics that I mentioned in that note.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, really, Mr. Cvijetic knows that none of this was covered. His interview says, I did nothing except have cups of coffee, effectively, all over the place. None of what is contained in this one line was ever dealt with in the interview. Now, Mr. Cvijetic can explain verbally now, if he wants to, what the Foca action is meant to cover, but it is to give us proper notice of what the witness is to say. That is the purpose of a proofing note. That gives us no indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, if I may add, the Chamber has, at several occasions, asked also to be given copies of the background information so as to allow the Chambers to familiarise themselves with the evidence before the witness appears in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm being informed that we submitted the witness interview and in that interview he speaks about the planned operation of the Special Police, and he also tried to locate it in time and state the reasons and so on. I listened to a tape recording of his statement several times and we submitted the interview too, and that is what I'm talking about. The relevant pages are 28, 29, and 30 of his interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the reference to it again. He was asked about war activities. But as far as I can see, it's nothing to do with Foca. In any event, Your Honours, my objection still stands, the whole thing. Foca has nothing to do with the indictment. Novo Sarajevo has nothing to do with the indictment. Foca, certainly, as Your Honours may know, there was a whole trial over what happened in Foca. And to start opening that up, Your Honours, you may think would not be of assistance to anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let us bring in the witness. But before the witness comes, the Chamber is mindful of the obligation of counsel to limit himself within the scope of the indictment. Now, Mr. Cvijetic, if you wish to embark upon anything that has to do with Novo Sarajevo or Foca, then you have to be offering to us an explanation as to just why you do so and what exactly it is that you wish to raise in relation to these two locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if the Prosecution is willing to give up the topic of the causes and reasons for the break-up of the former Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of socialist [as interpreted] Herzegovina, I will not deal with that topic. We are discussing the causes and reasons for the break-up of the MUP, and witnesses have been heard about that, and nobody has so far been prevented to testify about the events preceding that break-up. This witness would be the first one to be prohibited to speak about it. As for Foca, we will not discuss Foca but with the role and task of the Crime Prevention Department in the processing and prosecution of paramilitaries, their detention, et cetera, which also was the goal of a preceding action, the one in Zvornik, and that was also the goal of the one that was planned for Foca. His task was to lead the group of inspectors who were to lead the -- or who were to be members of the group for the processing of the perpetrators. I will only ask him about the preparations, his preparations for that operation, and that will be all because the operation never took place. We will never even enter Foca, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, allow me to say that all these discussions could probably have been avoided if we would have been provided with a proper proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Usher, please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Orasanin. Do I pronounce that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You do hear me in a language you understand, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your testimony. You are about to read a solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out that the solemn declaration that you are about to make does expose you to the penalties of perjury should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. Now then, would you please be kind enough to read aloud the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we begin by asking you to state your full name and your date and place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Milomir Orasanin. I was born on 8 June, 1954, in Zljebovi, which is in the municipality of Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb. I'm a Serb by ethnicity and an Orthodox Christian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what is your profession today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what was your occupation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 I was a crime prevention inspector in the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, sir, is this your first testimony before this Tribunal or have you ever testified before this Tribunal or in a tribunal of your country about these matters, the matters relating to the 1992 war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I'm giving evidence in a trial about these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay then. Let me explain to you briefly how the proceedings will unfold here. You have been called as a witness by the Defence for Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Cvijetic, who is sitting to your left, Mr. Cvijetic has asked for altogether eight or ten hours. I don't know whether the ten-hour request has already been made. And after Mr. Cvijetic finishes his examination-in-chief, Mr. Krgovic, who is Defence counsel for Stojan Zupljanin, will cross-examine you. And the OTP will cross-examine you. Which will take, in total, as we can estimate it for the moment, around five or six hours. After that, we give the floor once again to Mr. Stanisic Defence. And after that, and during the course of all other examinations, the Judges may have questions for you. There is a practical matter. The recordings of these proceedings are such -- the technical conditions are such that we need to take breaks every 90 minutes, and we'll take a break, a 20-minute break, after every 90 minutes. And we sit from 9.00 in the morning until a quarter to 2.00 every day. So that's all I have to say to you. And I give the floor to Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I don't know if Your Honours -- I'm sorry, I don't think Your Honours gave him a warning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, did you? Oh, I missed that, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I do it, Ms. Korner, before the witness reads the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I completely missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Orasanin.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you replied? I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do speak up so we can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, in the introductory portion of the examination-in-chief, it is common for a witness to tell us something about his life and resume, and I would appreciate it if you could tell the Trial Chamber chronologically when and where it was that you started working, what your career path was. And if you skip anything, then I will ask you about it, but please do try and speak in a paced manner.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, thank you. After I completed elementary school in 1973, I completed the Police Academy at the intermediate level and I worked as a police officer at this city SUP. In 1976 up until 1978, I went to a police academy at a college level and at that time I was appointed as junior inspector in the crime department. From 1981 or 1982 up until 1985, I went to university and I completed and received a university degree in political science, and I was appointed as deputy commander at a police station for public security in Novo Sarajevo, following which I was appointed as the chief of the Crime Prevention Department in Novo Sarajevo, and I remained in that post up until 1992, in other words, until the beginning of the war. In addition, I also worked, between is 1975 and 1976, as a clerk for crime prevention. Perhaps I skipped that portion, I don't know. So to just recap: When the war broke out, I was the chief of the Crime Prevention Department in Novo Sarajevo, and this Public Security Station was part of the Centre for Public Security in Sarajevo. When the war broke out in 1992, I worked as an inspector, a crime prevention inspector, in the newly-established administration of the RS MUP, and I remained in that post until, as far as I can recall, the 20th of November, 1992, when I was appointed commander or chief of the Department for Border Affairs, and I remained in that position up until the 11th of March, 1988 [as interpreted]. In 1988, I was the deputy of the chief of public security in Zvornik up until the 31st December, 1990 -- 2001. 2001, apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you here to clarify something in the transcript. It says here that you were appointed to this post in 1988; is that an error? Could you try and recall.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, in 1988 I was the chief of the Crime Prevention Department in the Public Security Station of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the question was when were you appointed to the Zvornik duty where you remained up until 2001 as you said?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, this came immediately after the election. The election -- the general elections were in 1997. And then in 1998, in March, I believe the letter of appointment said the 11th of March, I'm not -- I can't recall the exact date, but I think that's what it says there, and I remained in that duty up in until the 31st of December, 2001. That is my precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, no, no, the reason I interfere was because we had in the transcript "1988."

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, that's an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: In 2001, from December 31st, I was appointed to the Intelligence Security Service, and I remained there for three years, when a joint service was established for the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I retired in -- or, rather, I stopped working on 31st December, 2004, when I prepared for retirement and I became a pensioner. And I am no longer on active duty. I am a retired person and no longer work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How old were you when you started working?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, we started working right after elementary school. This was the first generation of the first class of the academy, the police academy, and I -- we were actually all accepted to work as junior police officers. We were still under age, practically. And when I turned 18, I began working in the full -- to the full extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can see, your entire career was in the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: That's correct. My entire career was within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can we please make sure that once I complete my question you just pause briefly and then start answering. Perhaps you can take a look at the screen and that should help you. If you can see, there's a cursor there.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, the usher will come and assist you in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, now I can -- I see the text before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, the police academy and your generation, your class, can you remember any other people who would later on be on higher positions in the Ministry of the Interior in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Could you just mention a few names that you went to school together?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies, but I just have to say that the text that I see before me is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, you will be able to figure out when I have completed my question and that's all you need. You don't need to see the text. So do you recall my question?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes. The question was who was in the first generation of the police academy, the cadets there. So I can name a few. Now, this was the first class that was graduated from the Ministry of the Interior school. It was multi-ethnic to reflect the national -- the ethnic structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I know that, for instance, Leotar, Jozo was in my generation, or, rather, Jozo Leotar. Ismet Dahic, Mico Stanisic, Momo Mandic, Tomislav Planojevic, then a man by the name of Stevanovic, Tomislav Vucic, Zivadin [as interpreted] Tutus, Azim Hurtic, Ahmed Mijazomic [phoen], and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to check whether Mr. Stanisic was in that same class, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, you did the job that you mentioned here and you remained in that job after the multi-ethnic elections. Did you observe any changes within the Ministry of the Interior after the multi-party elections, and, if so, could you tell us what kind of changes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for asking that. As I've already told you, I was the chief for crime prevention in Novo Sarajevo at the time. There were 14 to 15 inspectors who were my subordinates. This was a multi-ethnic group. There were Serbs, Croats, Bosniaks, and we all worked together as a team. It was a homogenous group. After the multi-party elections, our job was far more difficult in terms of security because we did our job within the framework of the law and it was our job to prevent crime, and we dealt with general crime and crimes against property, and we had numerous cases. We observed that in security terms the conditions of work were in jeopardy, so we were no longer able to work properly. In other words, we were between a rock and a hard place, if I can put it that way. There were criminals. Criminals became very prominent in those days. The courts and the prosecutors were inefficient. I don't know the reasons for that. And as for working conditions, we also did not have sufficient means to deal with the crime. We didn't have enough fuel or other equipment, especially forensic equipment, and all the other items that you need to use during an investigation. Later on, we observed that some criminal groups were acting jointly and they were homogenous. They were dominant at the time. And because of the difficulty in our work, we were actually unable to work efficiently. And as I've said a little earlier, and I can't recall all the names, but we did conduct analysis of all this and it was always the same groups that we arrested. And the event that had to do with the attack on the police station had -- was in that same vein. So all I can say is that we worked around the clock but the courts and the prosecutors were inefficient, ineffective in their work, and we had no resources for our work. There were -- well, before the war we called these groups organised criminal groups and they engaged both in crimes against property, that was the term, the legal term that was used, but there were also groups that were a bit more hardcore. They also engaged in robberies and aggravated crimes including violent conduct. I know that they had ties to some of our men because we could see them, people who still worked in our service. What I'm trying to say is that after the multi-party elections, various parties liked to promote their own men so that in effect we had no support. Alija Delimustafic became the head of the ministry. And all these people were party people. And I have to say, there were people from all ethnic groups. They all tried to push their own men forward so that we were left to our own resources and to our own devices in fighting the criminal groups. This was so on a daily basis. I can mention here Juka Prazina, Ismet Bajramovic Celo, whom I know personally because in 1982 I was an operative and I was in charge of a criminal investigation that was completed some six or seven months later, and this criminal group was indicted and they received very high sentences, prison sentence, but -- and this was in the former Yugoslavia. So that's why I know -- that's how I know these people. And I know that the minister, too, had ties to them because he used to be a police officer and then he left the service. So there were ties with Ismet Bajramovic Celo. But later on, perhaps, I can answer your questions, because I don't want to be too long in my reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you for a moment. Please tell us just a few words about the personnel policy within the ministry. Who was in charge for the personnel and human resources policy within the ministry after the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, as I've already mentioned, after the multi-party elections, in my assessment, but I don't know if I'm the competent person to speak about this, I'm just saying what I think, well, but in my view the personnel policy was bad. Some new people came on board and everyone tried to bring their own stooges, so that the personnel policy in the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP was conducted by Selmo -- by Hilmo Selimovic. Then there was Bruno Stojic who was chief of one of the administrations, I can't recall exactly which one. And then there was a Mirsad person. He was the key man in the personnel department. Hilmo Selimovic was in charge of the administration; he was a deputy minister. But his immediate subordinate was Mirsad Srebrenkovic who was the key personnel man, so that I know about some of their choices and some of the activities that they engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to ask you about those decisions, personnel appointments, that they actually made. What did they reflect, and did they in any way interfere with the personnel policy at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, it was obvious and it was a general rule, they didn't adhere to the criteria for the manning of the reserve police force. Everybody was taking on board their own people. The reserve police force was manned ad hoc. The procedure wasn't respected. I know that in the territory covered by our SJB it was like that, and the same goes for Stari Grad. The ethnic composition was not reflected. As far as I remember, only one or two Serbs were active-duty officers there. The chief of the police station was Ismet Dahic. In Novo Sarajevo, the commanders of the local communities were the most important people for security. Eighty per cent of the information from public security went through these people, the commanders of local communities and sector chiefs. In Novo Sarajevo there were only two Serbs and one Croat. There were 18 commanders of local communities or sector chiefs. And I noticed that the national -- or ethnic balance was tipped. It was very obvious. It wasn't a secret at all. We couldn't really operate in a homogenous manner as we did before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now, very briefly, did you have intelligence from that period about people being sent to police training in Croatia by the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, there was such intelligence. Actually, it was almost a public thing because we spoke about it. A group of officers was sent to Croatia for training, and it went through Mirsad. As far as I know, they later worked in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But there was a police training school at Vraca from which you graduated, so how do you explain the fact that a political party was sending candidates for police training? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment. I didn't object to the first leading question, "Did you have intelligence about that period about people being sent to police training in -- by the SDA party?" Now he asks: "How do you explain the fact that a political party was sending candidates for police training?" He didn't actually say that a political party had sent them for police training. He said somebody called Mirsad, whoever Mirsad may be, was sent to Croatia for training. So these questions must be asked in non-leading form. This is your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Who organised this training and who drafted or compiled the lists of candidates for the training?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was a parallel process that took place outside the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were located somewhere on Bascarsija and they acted through Ismet Dahic, but Mirsad was a MUP member. And it was upon their nomination that they were sent for training. That's the information I have. But Hilmo Selimovic was chief of the personnel administration, whereas Mirsad was also a personnel executive. So without them it wouldn't have been possible. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Mirsad several times. Please tell us his family name.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Srebrenkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will move on to the security situation. Not after the multi-party elections, but in 1992, immediately before, open war broke out. Did anything change with regard to security in 1992 in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes. When the security situation had been disrupted, we got information that some criminal groups were armed. I know that. I know some of them personally because I worked on [as interpreted] some of them, and they had ties with Musan Topalovic, Caco. He commanded one unit. I believe that they were 360 in all. They also had ties with Juka Prazina. I know Juka Prazina personally because our inspectors processed him a number of times and I was their superior. And as I said, one group had ties with Ismet Bajramovic, also known as Celo. Those groups were armed. Under the law or laws and regulations and the constitution, they should have been considered terrorist groups since they were armed. And our service was duty-bound to prevent their activities. And not only the activities of those groups, but any armed individuals. We were supposed to disarm them and process them. That was the general attitude. But before the war, and our police station was attacked on the night of the 4th, but before the war, or a day or two before, it was a time when I had some 15 operatives, Juka Prazina and his unit entered the police social centre, and on the following day the Novo Sarajevo Police Station was attacked. As far as I know, that group was led by one "Puska." I'm certain that they had come from Stari Grad in two vans and they changed in the immediate vicinity by the paramedical facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just tell us how that attack ended.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: One person was killed, and the duty police officer from the station was kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What's the name of the police officer who was killed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Pero Petrovic was killed, and Lazar Bojanic was on duty shift at the police station. Maybe I should clarify the role of the duty officer. At a police station, the duty officer is the most important person for monitoring the security situation in the territory when the commander and the deputy are absent, that is, after regular working hours. All information, all reports go through that person. He basically ran everything. The commander gave him assignments and there were people out on the beat patrolling and everybody else who was on that particular shift. In Novo Sarajevo, I think that there were 25 to 30 police officers in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's cut that short a bit. After these events, was it possible to remain in a joint MUP, for you personally?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, I was assessing the situation. And I have already said that there was -- we were a multi-ethnic organisation. There was mutual trust among Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats. Our ties never really broke, the ties among us. But we were all afraid of these criminal groups. We were supposed to process them. They all had their police files. There were several reports against each one of them. And no matter whether the detective from our ranks was a Bosniak, a Serb, or a Croat, he was afraid. Our premises were broken into, everything had been taken out, and we were afraid for our personal safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What is the immediate reason for your departure? Did these groups that you mentioned threaten you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, it was obvious. On the eve of the war, it was a weekend. I went to the country-side, that's what I usually did on weekends, and I made or drafted a schedule of operative work, but then a group broke into the station, and Zeljko Rakic was the duty officer at the time. He saw all that. He was -- he wanted to cross the street but then he noticed a man in the shadow by a bank. That's the night when that murder happened. And the offices were broken into. All documents were taken out. And then I understood that I wasn't safe and that there was no place for me anymore. I didn't return. Later, somebody broke into my apartment in Dobrinja. I don't know if I should speak about it now or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This will do for the time. After this burglar entered your apartment and these events, what ensued? Did you stay in Sarajevo? And when did you leave?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: As I said, just before that event it so happened that I went to the country-side with my family and I stayed there for two or three weeks. My apartment was broken into some 10 or 15 days after that, so I felt unsafe and I understood that there was no place for me there anymore. I understood that there was no reason for me to go back to my office because whatever we had done before we were unable to continue doing. And it wouldn't have been logical for me to return to the office where I used to work. And that's what the others did, too. I was afraid for my safety. Afraid for my life, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you - and, if so, when - join the newly-established MUP of the RS?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I spent three or four weeks in the country-side. And later, as time passed by, I learned that the RS MUP was being established. And it was a logical thing. To my mind there were two options: either you go for the MUP or for the army. I opted for the MUP because that's all I can do. And I think I'm trained for that kind of job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When did you actually report to work at the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was in early May. I don't remember the exact date, but it was in early May. I'm sure of that. It may have been on the 3rd or 4th. I found Cedo Kljajic there and some others. And the decision of my appointment was dated April, but I only reported for work in May. That period was not covered. It was still the organisational phase.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Who did you find there, I mean, the personnel, and what were the working conditions like at the newly-established MUP? Where did you go, who did you find there, what did you do, what kind of materiel and equipment did you have and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for asking. It was the very beginning. And as for the working conditions, well, there weren't really any working conditions at all. I found Cedo Kljajic there, Dobro Planojevic. And Dobro said to me that Mico Stanisic was minister, that a crime enforcement administration was being set up, but there was a shortage of personnel. We didn't have any equipment there, no vehicles, no materiel. We were told to sit in the Kalovita Brda facility; that's at Pale. It was some sort of a scouts facility. There were a couple of offices there, a telephone, and that's about it. Dobro said to me that the minister had ordered that we should establish a professional crime enforcement administration and that we should find personnel. It was the very start. And that was our task that followed from the order of the minister and the laws and regulations. And I asked, Well, how do we go about it? We don't even have a typewriter. And then he said, Well, we'll find a way. And then he said that at Energoinvest in Lukavica there was something. And I brought a typewriter from there. So we started from scratch actually. And three services were to begin operating: the police administration headed by Vlastimir Kusmuk, then the crime enforcement service headed by Dobro Planojevic, and national security. I think it was headed by Slobodan Skipina. We had four men at the very beginning. I, Dobro, we were later joined by Nikola Milanovic. Later on I'll speak about personnel. There was Ratko Kapetanovic and Milan Ostojic. We were looking for people because we were short of people. And the orders were clear, and they were based on the law and the minister's order. But as I said, we started from scratch. So we had a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll show you a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't know where we're going with this, but I would suggest that you focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, I will show you a document. That's a 65 ter document. 10D1. That's under tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my apologies, if I could have the assistance of the usher to provide this binder to the witness. I don't think we have the right document. We need 65 ter 10D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: This document 120?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Don't mind the numbers. Just look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Is this under number 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, tab 3. So here we see a list of employees who worked in the Ministry of the Interior at the headquarters in May, in the month of May. And as we can see, there is a breakdown according to administration. At the bottom of page 1, we see the Crime Prevention Administration; is that your administration?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes. If you allow me to explain, this is the Crime Prevention Administration. We see that there's Dobrisav Planojevic. It says here that he's assistant minister. And then we have Goran Macar, co-ordinator; Nikola Milanovic, inspector; Milomir Orasanin, inspector. This was in the month of May, in other words, in the early days of establishing the Crime Administration, and this is a list of employees for the month of May. There is no need to comment on it. Now, we also see the Police Administration; that's the other administration or service that was at Kalovita Brda. Then there's Vladimir -- we see Vlastimir Kusmuk, Milos Zuban --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You don't need to read. So we see there were only four men in your administration; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you recall what kind of work you did at that time, in the month of May, your administration?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, in the month of May our job was really just to orientate ourselves in -- during the process of establishing the Crime Prevention Administration. That means that we were supposed to draw up a kind of blueprint in order to operate within the bounds of the law. We were preparing the departments, employment, various regulations that we had to abide by that related to the Crime Prevention Department. The legal -- the regulations and the bylaws had not been drawn up yet. They were still -- we were still in the process of preparing all those documents. They had to do with the work of the Crime Prevention Administration, but we were in the process of drawing up various documents, legal documents, that actually guided the work of the Crime Police Administration. But because we had insufficient means and resources, our first task was to try and get the right personnel. So we were looking for people who could work as inspectors in the field in public security stations and public security centres; however, there were problems in that because we could not really go out in the field. And I will get back to this a little later to explain what kind of difficulties were there. But as far as I can recall, this was pursuant to an order from the minister, Minister Stanisic, who told him that we had a free hand, that we could set up our administration in any way we wished, and that it should work within legal provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if there are no objections, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it would be a bit otiose because if Mr. Cvijetic looks at P867, you'll see the same document but with signatures, which seems to be slightly more appropriate than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document that I'm tendering is a seven-page document, and it contains and lists all administrations within the Ministry of Interior. The document that Ms. Korner is referring to is a two-page document. Now, if you look at this, you will see that there are listed all administrations at the headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior, and what is relevant here is that we see the structure of the ministry in those early days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And to what end is it being offered, Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I should add, most of it's crossed out of this document, so I don't know how much that's going to help. There's actually crossings through - one, two, three - three of the seven pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've already stated that from these seven pages we can see the number of services and administrations within the Ministry of the Interior at the headquarters, and we also see what the personnel situation was. So this is why I'm tendering this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, we are inclined to let the document in, but we are concerned about the crossed out pages to which Ms. Korner has referred. Is there someone who is in a position to enlighten us on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, would you please look at the pages where we see that some portions were crossed out. Do you have any information, do you know anything about whether all of these services and administrations actually existed in the compositions as shown here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, first of all, it ought to come up on the screen. Secondly, that's a leading question. The simple question is, Do you have an explanation for the crossings-out? Not your own ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, please take a look at page 5. You can see the "Crime Prevention Service" there.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Is that under tab 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, the same tab, tab 3, but just leaf through the pages. Yes, and it's crossed out.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, find the page beginning with the name Goran Macar.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, in my binder, that's page 3, F190897.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you know why this was crossed out? Was this the composition, the personnel situation, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, this is a list of workers who worked in the month of May 1992 and received an advance on their pay salary for the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, just answer my question: Do you know what the crossing out refers to and whether this is an actual authentic list?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, what I see here is a list of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, take a look at the right-hand side of the page, where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, I see here, for instance, Rajko Bujic was from Ilidza. Ljuboje, Mirko also he used to be -- he is a former -- Mirko Ljuboje is a former employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So is this information correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, at the seat -- this information is correct. Zoran Mihajlovic, Novo Sarajevo. Simo Tusevljak, Sasa Blagojevic, I know them. Orasanin, Novo Sarajevo. All of them. Majstorovic, Luko; Zeljko Vasiljevic. So this list is complete. Dejan, yes. All these were operatives who were employees before the war, and they were now listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What about number 8?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, that's correct, that's a MUP Novo Sarajevo, me, Milomir Orasanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment. It says Mico Orasanin; is that you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, that's -- this is an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [no interpretation] ...

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: This is me, but it's an error. This Mico is the nickname that is used for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. What about the right-hand column where it says where you came from; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, in the right-hand column, is that where all these men had come from, and it was entered by hand?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is the information correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, if you allow me, there are some errors here. For instance, Rajko Vukovic, that's an error. It says Ilidza and it should be Novo Sarajevo. So it was actually erroneously entered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But did he work in Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Mirko Ljuboje, too, but not at the headquarters. This is a list of employees who were in the crime service, but the list -- the list that we saw earlier was in the Crime Prevention Administration, a list of employees of the Crime Prevention Administration, and that is what explains the discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is then the explanation for the crossing out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us why this was done in this manner?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. For instance, Rajko Gluhovic, I see there was -- it's indicated here that he came from Ilidza, but in fact it should be Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I stand by my earlier request to have this document tendered into evidence. This is the document that we have. We don't have any other. And it shows the full staffing of the Ministry of the Interior at the headquarters. So it's up to you now. I leave it to you, to your discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D569, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see the time, and perhaps we are already late for the break, so I propose that we take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Orasanin, we will be taking our first break as indicated by Judge Delvoie, so we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, you may continue, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, I will now focus on your administration from the organisational aspect, and I'm going to show you a number of documents so we may see how the manning of your administration went.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see document 8D1. That's a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... tab, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 4. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, this is a list of employees of the crime administration for the month of June. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was there an increase in the number of inspectors, at least according to this list?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from Dobrislav Planojevic, Goran Macar, Nikola Milanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do read names more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Milomir Orasanin; Rade Miladinovic, who is under number 5; Petko Pekic; Borka Kovacevic, she's a typist; Milka Cosic; and Danilo Vukovic, who is also an inspector. Which adds up to a total of nine new employees in the crime administration. This is a list from June.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the employee, but I was interested in the inspectors. But the only one who's called an inspector is Danilo Vukovic under 9?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, Danilo Vukovic. He is an inspector with a college degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you got a new inspector who -- under number 9, Danilo Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes. And the others do other jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So do you agree that this is a list of all employees of the crime administration at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, this is the basic administration that was located at Kalovita Brda.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, do we not have this information already? I seem to recall the names of Dobrislav Planojevic and Goran Macar from the previous document, and I'm not quite sure what is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a list for the following month, for June. And I wish to show how the manning strength of that administration grew. The one we have seen was for May, and this is for the following month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D570, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see document 1D065476.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we have a tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is tab 5, Your Honour. Your Honours, I just want to draw your attention to the fact that we wanted to add this document on a 65 ter list because it was only disclosed to us recently, and its number was 900D1. So if I may, I will comment on it with the witness and then we'll see about the inclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, we'll move on to the following month, July. We can see some personnel changes again, or, rather, can you see any new inspectors on the list? I'm interested in inspectors only. Can you see any new names there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for this question. Yes, I remember this list. This was in July. I think that Dobro told me to type it up with the typist. These are the same people only reinforced by Ljubomir Kovacevic and Zeljko Vasiljevic. It includes the existing inspectors and then other personnel plus these two new arrivals.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you said that you personally compiled this list, there's no need for me to ask you how you know it.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember exactly. Planojevic told me, Go ahead and do it. And I did it with Borka, so I really remember this list for July.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the same reasons as the previous document, I seek to tender this one as well. Or, rather, first to include it in our list according to our previous submission and then I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, on the list that I have from you listing the documents that you're going to use with this witness, tab 5 is already in evidence. It's Exhibit P1437.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will check, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, we understand the pattern that you have shown in terms of May, June; we are now up to July. How much farther are you going with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only two more months, Your Honour. I'm just following the witness's presence in this administration and simultaneously the manning of that administration and enabling it to go about its work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, in the Chamber's view, this document ought not to be admitted because it's unnecessary for the reason that the -- we have the -- what I would call the basic document which has previously been admitted. And the witness has explained, for instance in relation to the document presently up on the screen, July, that you look at the basic document and there are these changes. We don't need the document because we have the exhibit as qualified in respect of subsequent months by the witness's oral testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it does not explain what the purpose is for showing these documents. The reason why I'm showing them is the development of the manning strength of a very important organisational unit as well as the level of manning throughout 1992. They started off with only four inspectors, but I want to show how that unit developed and by which time it became an organisational unit with the adequate number of personnel. Not merely to point out the initial situation because we have seen that already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Unless I'm missing something, Mr. Cvijetic, the witness's testimony on this point is how you have established that, and we don't see how adding a piece of paper adds to what the witness has positively testified to already. We have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Your Honours, I will just show these lists, then, and have the witness comment on them without tendering them after that. That is not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order not to waste any more time, let us move on to document 1D065479. It was -- it was to be included in our 65 ter list as 901D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, have you opened tab 6? I omitted to state the tab number. Take a look at this list, please. I will ask you the question. It's about inspectors again. Are there any new inspectors as compared to the previous list? And if any, please tell us who they are.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: There is one additional staff and that is Ranko Vasiljevic, but he's -- or, rather, Ranka Vasiljevic, who is not an inspector. And this document is important because there was a change in the Crime Prevention and Detection Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just tell us whether there was a rise in the number of inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, Ranka Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Since this document will not be admitted into evidence, please tell us the date, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: This is a payroll for the month of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, there is something wrong here. The witness testified that Ranka Vasiljevic is not an inspector. That's line 16 on page 34. And yet when you asked whether there was a rise in the number of inspectors subsequently, the witness answers: "Yes, Ranka Vasiljevic." So is this person an inspector or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, please answer the question of the Judge. You have created confusion.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, Ranka Vasiljevic was an administrator in the Crime Prevention and Detection Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please focus on the question, sir. Has there been a rise in the number of inspectors, and, if so, who are the new inspectors as compared to the previous month? I believe the question is clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: No, there has been no rise in the number of inspectors in this month as compared to the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not tender this document. Instead we will move on to the month of September. Could we please see 65 ter 37D1. That's tab 7, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, please look at the list for September. And my question is the same again: Is there an increase in the number of inspectors? And if so, tell us who the new arrivals are.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: In this document for September 1992, there is a rise in the number of inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please say the names slowly.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Sinisa Karan, with a university degree; Dragomir Peric, post-secondary education; Ostoja Minic, likewise; Savka Lazic, likewise; Mitar Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just tell us who the new inspectors are.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Mitar Lukic, Radenko Milicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Orasanin, I see your name in third place. I do not have any later payrolls, so tell us, How long did you effectively work in this administration?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I was on their list up until 20 November 1992. So this is September 1992, while I was still on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you remember if you were on the list in October and received your salary as an employee of that administration?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I probably was. But if I really received my salary, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, can you tell me briefly, just in a couple of sentences, what the basic role and the task of the -- of an Administration for Crime Prevention and Detection in the Ministry of the Interior is? Just give us a brief outline of your basic tasks. And now I'm referring to inspectors specifically.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: The basic tasks of the Crime Prevention Administration are to apply the regulations within their jurisdiction, regulations linked to crime prevention. This administration has an instructive jurisdiction and it also monitors the work of other crime services at public security centres and public security stations. These are some legal obligations which follow from legal regulations, primarily from the Law on the Interior instructions on crime prevention and detection and certain other instructions. So our main goal is to prevent and detect crime, with the assistance of other organs such as the prosecutor's office and the courts. And we assist these organs; this is the basic function. And that was the basis of our work in 1992 when we were contemplating the formation of the Crime Prevention Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Among others, you mentioned some instructive duties. What does that imply?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Instructive tasks in this field -- and I must say that at the time we just took over previous regulations, and in 1992 this was all in a phase of legal regulations being created, because we simply took over some regulations that were valid previously in Bosnia-Herzegovina and our work simply followed from these. These instructions are an auxiliary document, and they assist the work of the Crime Prevention Administration. There are certain obligations listed in there which applied to all levels of this administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. On page 37, line 10, you mention the prosecutor's office and the courts, and it didn't -- it wasn't recorded what you did in relation to the courts and the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, we assist them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Nothing more, we just wanted to correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will show you a document, and I would like to have - this is an exhibit, I believe - P988. P988, please. It's tab 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this document, the title of which is "Inspection Checklist," and please pay attention to what the inspection checklist actually contains. Please look at the bullet points.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: This document --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you look at the document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you some questions. Sir, when you look at everything that a complete inspection includes, could you tell us how many employees and from which services of the ministry would be involved in such an inspection?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: This document talks about the manner of work and inspection and crime services; namely, for such work you would need two or three inspectors who would be able to examine the entire situation in the crime prevention administration of a certain area or the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please wait for the question. Does this type of inspection -- is this type of inspection something that was also done in the previous system in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, it was done in the same way. And the regulations were taken over. This was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question was --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: It was the same before as in this inspection checklist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As an inspector and as a member of a team, did you go to carry out inspections in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: My answer is yes. However, when we left the Crime Prevention Centre, our main task would be to change the regulations [as interpreted], to establish what the situation was. However, when we arrived in the field, we found that the situation was completely different. Crime services where I visited were either poorly organised or not organised at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In line -- page 39, line 6, it says -- line 5 it says that you were to change the regulations, but I believe you said to apply regulations.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, to apply regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Were you ever in a situation in 1992 to conduct such a full inspection, as this document states, and to carry out everything that is listed in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, in 1992, when we visited some places such as Doboj, Foca, Skelani, and other places, in some places the situation that we found was according to the regulations. There were records and so on. But there were problems that differed from place to place. It depended on the organisation and on staffing levels. In some places there were some shortcomings, the situation differed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: According to you, how much time would have been needed for such an inspection to be carried out in a certain SJB in accordance with this regulation?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, the regulations are clear. First you have to announce to the SJB or to the CSB that MUP inspectors were arriving, and for that you need technical abilities, so you need to have communications in order to let them know that you were arriving. That's what the regulations say. However, in 1992 this wasn't possible. The rule was for the inspectors to announce their arrival. They would be given tasks by their supervisors. And then these instructions would contain what needed to be done. However, you would need at least two or three days to carry out a full inspection. You would need two or three inspectors to be present. However, I must also say that in 1992 this wasn't possible due to a lack of means, et cetera. There were some problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll ask you specific questions. What was your primary goal in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Our primary goal was to record the situation, to see about staffing levels. In some places the conditions were not met. In some places there weren't enough employees. And we wanted to see whether there were criminal records. It was a primary obligation to have log-books in the crime service and to apply legal powers which were set down in the Law on the Interior and the rules of the SJB. That was the primary goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When you went to the field, so to speak, were you given instructions about what you were supposed to take to the SJBs that you were visiting? And if so, please tell us what the basic instructions were that you had been given.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, as I said, the primary instructions were to record the situation and to make sure that the SJB can function, to see about their activities, and to see about whether they met the conditions, and whether they operated in accordance with instructions. That was the primary task that we had been given by the assistant minister Dobrislav Planojevic, who contacted Minister Stanisic and had been given this task. In the field, the situation we found was somewhat different, and there were problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned the field, I have to ask you: Were you obliged to file a report on the situation that you found in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. That was our obligation after our departure. It's a part of instructive inspection, to file a report. It's an obligation. There was only one case when we didn't send a report, and I will expand on that later, why we didn't file a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to specific visits to SJBs, I'll ask you this: Were you able to carry out a full inspection such as we can see in the document in any of your visits to the field?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That's already been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, your objection wasn't interpreted to me. Your microphone wasn't on. I'm not sure whether there was an objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've said that's already been asked and answered. And it was asked at page 39, line 13: "Were you ever in a situation in 1992 to conduct such a full inspection, as this document states, to carry out everything that is listed in this document?" And the answer follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeated the question because the witness didn't give a specific answer. I want to hear a specific answer from him. If you look at the answer, you'll see that it's not precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, please give me a specific answer to my question. And you heard the question. Were you able to carry out a full inspection in any of the stations that you visited, and, if so, where?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: In 1992 we were at the Doboj CSB and we recorded the situation, and I believe that there some sort of instructive control was carried out. And then we went to Foca and Visegrad, where records were compiled. As for the others, they were perfunctory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So what would you call the visits that you made to other stations where you didn't carry out a full inspection?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I suggested, since the instructor function according to the rules is obligatory, many activities follow from it, such as the reminder on inspection, and so we sent documents to various SJBs. I'm talking about this because there was a shortage, shall we call it a visit to SJBs. We didn't call it an instructive inspection because it implies lots of obligations, which relates to the places where this instructive inspection is carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will ask you whether you recall, and I will call it as you called it, this first visit, and I will ask you to describe what this visit actually looked like and what you did.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: As for the visits, I can't recall some of the dates or I might have got them mixed up because it was a long time ago. And when I talked to the investigator, I wasn't really prepared. I didn't want to use notes to remind myself, so I think I might have got some dates mixed up. I believe that first we went -- I believe I said we went to Ilijas and Vogosca, whereas first we went to Skelani, Zvornik, Brcko, and that area. And it was later that we visited Ilijas and Vogosca. And then after that we visited Doboj and Visegrad and Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: During the first visit you mentioned Bijeljina along with Brcko; can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. So we'll deal with your first visit, then. Can you recall as of these first four locations, what was the first place that you went to?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I must tell you that as we were leaving the MUP there were always problems with vehicles and with materiel. I can't remember who finally gave us a vehicle, but members of the team were Drago Borovcanin and Petko Pekic. And we went --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, members of your team, as for the members of the team, who went on behalf of which service?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Drago Borovcanin represented the uniformed police, and Petko and I went on behalf of the Crime Prevention Administration. There were two inspectors from the Crime Prevention Administration and one inspector from the Uniformed Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now can you remember my first question: Can you remember what your first destination was? Where did you go first?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I must tell you that after so much time -- but I know that we went from Sarajevo, that is, Pale, and then there is some 150 kilometres to the Drina. We crossed the Drina, we went to Zvornik, we spent two or three hours there, then we went to Brcko and Bijeljina, because that was the itinerary. We spent one night with relatives because there were no conditions for our work. We didn't have daily allowances, so we had to find accommodation. We visited the police station in Skelani, which was a newly-formed police station. And on our way back, we had a traffic accident. I don't know how it happened. I don't know whether it was staged or not staged. It's difficult for me to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Before I ask you what you found in the police stations, tell me, Did you put together a report on this visit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: We did go to those stations, only spent a couple of hours in Zvornik. It was an ad hoc visit. In the territory where those stations were, the ministry wasn't really up and running, and it wasn't operational. We didn't do our work because it wasn't possible. Instead, we dealt with who was on the job, trying to staff the crime prevention and detection service, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. The question was: Did you write and submit a report after your visit? Now you can answer.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: No, we didn't because we had a traffic accident and the colleague had to be taken to hospital. That's why we didn't write a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then let's see what you saw there, what the situation was. If you don't know the exact date, can you tell us roughly when you when on that visit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I'm certain that it was mid-May or late May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. My question is, Did you go to Zvornik at that period and were you able to?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: When we went to Zvornik, not the town itself because it wasn't safe, we stayed at Karakaj, it's a cross-roads. That's where we stayed, and we visited the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Who did you find in Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, I can only tell you what I know. We stayed there for an hour or two. In my opinion, they were totally disorganised. They weren't operational. The police station didn't have executive personnel. There was Marinko Vasilic and Petko Panic. The people there were all frightened. As far as I know, the Crisis Staff appointed some people there. Those were the most important problems. I personally spoke to Marinko Vasilic in front of the building because there weren't any conditions really there. They didn't have a functioning police station. It was only a couple of offices on the premises of a company. I think it was called Standard. And I suggested to him that he become the commander of the police station because there was a complete disorganisation and we wanted to include them into our structure legally.
