And that's actually more what we focused on rather than dealing with crime prevention problems, because it wasn't possible. I tried to persuade him to start running the police station because it was better for him to do it as a professional than somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned the local Crisis Staff as the institution that appointed people. Do you know who was appointed by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was an elderly man at the time, Pantelic I believe his name was, but I don't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where he was from?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I think that he hailed from Loznica. He may have been a pensioner already. He was so old that at the time I thought that he was no longer physically capable of doing the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Having mentioned Loznica, do tell us where that town is, the place where he hailed from.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Loznica is in Serbia, some 30 kilometres or so from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you observe that the MUP had decided to appoint chiefs of SJBs, and when and how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: After that traffic accident, we didn't work for a while. But I know that it was some two or three months later, as far as I remember, after the arrest of that paramilitary group, the Yellow Wasps. All decisions on appointment at the time were temporary, but that's when the first --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, don't -- let's leave that issue aside now. Just tell us the name of the first man in that position.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: The first chief of the SJB there, and I think it was July, his name was Milorad Lokancevic, who was appointed pursuant to a decision of the ministry, and it was a temporary decision, as far as I remember. I know the man. I met him later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about Mr. Pantelic, which position were you discussing all the time? That is, which position was he in?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't really remember all details, because when we stayed there briefly, we couldn't even sit down at the office and talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: He was chief of the SJB of Zvornik, so he was the number one man for the -- for policing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Apart from the organisational work and the staffing matters, you weren't really in a position to do what you were supposed to do about the crime prevention and detection service?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can answer that question. We didn't even go to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I anticipate your objection. I know it's leading, but the witness actually said it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It doesn't make it any better. And I don't think he did say it. You cannot really ask a question that says, You weren't really in a position to do what you were supposed to do. He gives the evidence, not you, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. [Interpretation] All right. I understand. Let me phrase it this way:

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Were you able to do the work you had set out to do?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: No. And that's only logical because the police station wasn't really properly organised. We only found five or six people there who weren't really organised. They didn't even have a premises. Their proper premises were in Zvornik, so we couldn't really do the job in that one hour that we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It was recorded that you said that the police station wasn't properly organised, but you said that it didn't really exist?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, it did exist in three offices, but it wasn't really organised as a service to function in accordance with the laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'm sorry, I'm being pedantic about this, but the rule that's being followed is that if something has been mistranslated, then the witness is asked to repeat it, not that Mr. Cvijetic, counsel, tells him what he said. So that should be followed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept your objection. That's how I'll proceed from now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, what did you see in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: The three of us visited Skelani. Skelani was -- Skelani became a municipality at the time. Before the war, there was a police substation, not really an SJB. We went there and we knew the man who I think also was chief of the Crisis Staff there. He -- we talked to him and found out that the Crisis Staff had established a police station, because before the war there had only been a police substation or branch police station actually, so they had appointed some of their own people there. We discussed that and made it clear that it must be in line with the laws and regulations governing the work of the ministry. There were about a dozen police officers or so. I can't remember. We spoke to the commander and said that it must be clear whether they are eligible or not, and then we got a list. It wasn't really our job. We were crime prevention and detection inspectors. But on the other hand there was nothing else for us to do. So we wanted to make sure that the police station is established in line with the laws and regulations governing the work of the ministry. There were always problems with staffing. We would nominate some people, but the local -- locals didn't like that, the powers that be, as it were, and that's how it was in Skelani and everywhere else. That was the constant bone of contention between the local authorities and the official structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You never said who -- what the name of the man was who ran that branch police station.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: It was Marko Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please wait for my question. Did he state the reasons for the Crisis Staff establishing a branch police station or police station proper?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I must wait for the cursor, yes. I was able to speak to him because I had known him from before. He was a police officer and had worked as such and then he retired. I asked him, What is this all about? because I didn't understand the situation. How do you select your personnel? And then he replied, If we waited for you to do it, we would be in a position to have to flee across the Drina. They -- his reply was -- or, rather, I said, But they must be employees of the ministry, responsible people, to live up to their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just a bit of patience. I'm interested in his explanation why the Crisis Staff had done it that way. And what became of that man? Did he remain in his position?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I don't really remember the dates. But on one occasion when he was fleeing Skelani, he was killed on the bridge over the Drina. According to the information I got from some police officers, he didn't want to withdraw in time, so he was killed while he was crossing the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But tell us, just in one sentence, who attacked Skelani? What kind of operation was it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: That was just one of about a dozen operations that are well known. It was an action conducted by Naser Oric, who attacked Skelani with his unit. I think that a village was torched in the process. He didn't want to leave among the first; he stayed there until the end and then he got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How many victims were there in that operation?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a date, please, before we go on with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when that action took place, when this man was killed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say. It may have been in late 1992 or early 1993. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's deal with something that you have just mentioned, that you took a list of the employees who were there at the time. And you said that although it wasn't your job, you wanted to turn them into MUP personnel. And so explain to us what the procedure is, in essence; how are such decisions issued?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I must say that not only there in Skelani, but elsewhere too, although now I can't remember the exact places, there were police officers who were not under our command. As far as I remember, we were couriers and drivers rather than inspectors, really, because there was total disorganisation. That's what I witnessed. We took those lists. We considered that to be our duty. But it was actually the work of Drago Borovcanin, because he was a uniformed police inspector. But it was actually me who made that suggestion to take those lists and check the procedures and see whether those police officers were eligible, and if so, that they should be issued decisions on their appointment. All these being temporary. I think I also had lists from Milici and Sekovici and some other stations. But there were no communication lines, and there was no courier service either. So that was actually the bulk of our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do explain why the decisions on appointment were temporary.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: For the simple reason that it wasn't possible to vet all those people or actually apply the provisions of the labour law that sets out the general conditions for work in the police. It wasn't even possible to check them, see if they have police files. It was the minister's decision and the assistant minister's. I wasn't at the collegium though. But I know that it was decided that they should be given temporary appointments before they become full professionals, because there was special conditions in place for the MUP, for employment with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do wait for my question. Which regulation of the MUP lays down the conditions for a future employee of the ministry in order to become appointed? What regulation is that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, as far as I recall, this document follows from the Law on Internal Affairs. Rules of procedure are passed of the Ministry of the Interior, and these rules of procedure prescribe certain special conditions for the employment of people in the ministry. And then it's on the basis of these special conditions that they have special obligations. Once an employee of the MUP receives a decision, then according to the regulations and according to the rules of procedure on internal structure, this person has certain rights but also has certain obligations. The rights are that he would get a salary, he would get annual leave, and other rights that follow from the labour law. Whereas the obligations are to apply all the regulations, all police powers, which also follow from the Law on Internal Affairs and from the rules of procedure on public security. These are obligations. This is why the decisions were all temporary, because there's a lot of responsibility there. And our leadership realised that they were taking on a large risk if they issued decisions without properly checking everybody. When we went on our visits - I can't call it an inspection - we noticed that there were some wild people, so to call them, who had our identity cards. At one check-point we showed our old identity cards and there was somebody from the military police there. He said, Never mind about that, I have that as well. And it was a blank official identity card. I was really astonished. These were probably some of the reasons why all the decisions were temporary. There was a lot of responsibility in giving a permanent decision to somebody for work in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of this internal document of the MUP. It wasn't recorded. Could you please tell us slowly.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: It's the Rules of Procedure on Internal Organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, in 19 -- was it passed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: These legal documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Or was it being worked on?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: All these legal documents, as far as I recall, in the field of the crime service --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer me.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it at the time. I didn't see that we had it at the time. If we had, we would have had some kinds of instructions. It was -- it would have been drafted after I left the crime administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the status of those who didn't have any decisions. Formally, legally, were they members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: No, they were not members of the MUP formally or legally, nor did they have any powers or obligations. They could not apply any police powers. They couldn't exercise any police powers. That was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was there also a problem with the fact that if they didn't have these decisions -- actually, could any proceedings be instigated against them if they didn't have these decisions?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that the decisions issued by the MUP implied that you had duties and obligations. However, if you weren't a member of the MUP, then you didn't have these obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I believe that we're done as far as Skelani is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should move on to Brcko and Bijeljina now, so, I don't know, Your Honours, whether we should start with these two municipalities because they're rather large.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We could be shorter about Bijeljina, so maybe you could tell us about how long you spent in Bijeljina and what you did there.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, as for Bijeljina, we hadn't really planned to be there. We had planned to be in Brcko and see about things in Brcko. The plan was that to get -- on our way back, since you had to pass through Bijeljina to go to Zvornik, we would drop by in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. So before the break, can you tell us what you did specifically in Bijeljina, what you found there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, I thought we should do it chronologically, since we first went to Brcko and this was on our way back and there was an unpleasant incident there. But we went to the police station in Bijeljina. None of the chiefs were there. We found the chief of legal affairs who had nothing to do with the operatives. There were no people there, so we had coffee with him. His name was Grkinic. He saw us, we had coffee with him. However, as for the job that we had come to do, he couldn't help us with because he was dealing with legal and administrative affairs, so we continued on our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since I'm going to move on to Brcko municipality and I believe I'll spend some more time there because it's rather important, I would like to suggest that we take a break a minute or two before and then we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. So we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way back in, Mr. Krgovic, we are reminded that we have yet to receive your estimates for cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's because -- [microphone not activated] ... Your Honours, it's because we don't have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, you may continue, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, if you remember, before the break we mentioned Brcko, so I would like to ask you to tell us briefly how long you stayed in Brcko, what you found there, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: We passed through Bijeljina and we went to Brcko. As far as I know, there were some combat operations around the town, so the town itself looked like there had been a war. That's what I could see on my way into town. We went to the police station. As far as I know, the chief wasn't there. Instead an inspector was there whose name was Gavrilovic. His brother worked at the Crime Prevention Administration of the Bosnian MUP, I believe. And I think that his name was Pero or Petar. We went there and we talked to him. The crime service there wasn't organised. I believe that he was in charge of some tasks, whether it was state security or something. I didn't know him before the war. So anyone who I didn't know before, I was a little bit careful with. But we didn't do anything special there. When we arrived, we were quite hungry because when we went to the field we didn't get any daily allowance or anything, so this man took us out to lunch. I can't remember exactly, I believe that we went on foot from the police station to the hotel, which is some hundred metres away, I think. There was a sniper that was shooting. Drago Borovcanin was there, I was there, and Gavrilovic. I should tell you that I found it all a little suspicious because there were few ricochets some ten metres from us. The ricochets went around, hits the asphalt, and then you, I found that a little suspicious. You can't say that I was afraid, but I was afraid, and there were a few such shots. We went inside to have a bite to eat, and on our way back I believe that Pekic left the car there. I can't remember the details. I know that we walked from the police station and the car was in front of the hotel. We noticed that we had a flat tire. We thought that we had a flat tire, so we wanted to find assistance to get a new tire and we replaced it. We put the flat tire in the boot and we went back. The duty officer was there and Gavrilovic was at the police station. As far as I recall, nobody else was there. That was the reason that we stayed a short time. Practically we gave up on any sort of work. And when we returned and came to Bijeljina, I said this before the break, that we spent some time in Bijeljina, however, our goal was to continue on our way, because Brcko is some 200 kilometres or even more away from Pale. So as we went to a mechanic to check the tire and to replace it, he told us that the tire didn't just burst but that somebody released all the air from it through the vent. That was our time in Brcko, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you received an explanation from Mr. Gavrilovic as for why everything was empty and what was happening in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: As far as I recall, and I don't want to guess or I don't want to make a mistake, but it seemed to me that this man was afraid. He was afraid. I knew that his brother had either already gone or was planning to go to Austria, to Vienna, and I think he was also contemplating leaving. I think he was afraid of some people there who also prepared this sabotage for us. It was later that some things turned out clearly. This is just my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What kind of people are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time that I spent there, that hour, hour and a half. I didn't know at the time. I could tell that he was afraid. He said there were some people there but we didn't go into any detail. I assumed that he was afraid, that people were afraid there. There might have been about a dozen people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll ask you about paramilitary -- was he referring to paramilitary formations in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, he mentioned them, but we didn't go into any details exactly because of the snipers. We just went to the police station. And because we were hungry, as far as I recall he said, Let's go and grab a bite and we'll talk about it there. And then on the way, I told you what happened. And I believe I might have initiated that we pull back to Bijeljina and have somebody else do the job later on. That is, there was a second team that we ran into on our way, and they were going from Sarajevo. I believe Vukovic was among them. And Dragan Andan was with them. I told Vukovic about these things and I told him this so they wouldn't be afraid, but I was primarily concerned about my own safety and I told this to Danilo Vukovic. After three, four, or five days, as far as recall, they went to Bijeljina and they visited the area. This was five, six, or ten days later. First they went to Bijeljina to get accommodated. I know that we ran into them at a well, they were drinking some water, and that's the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll just ask you shortly, Did you know that later on there was an operation carried out in Brcko, an operation of disarming the paramilitaries that you mentioned? Did you know about that or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: What I was talking about was around that time, around that date. I know that this was after our departure. I know that when these people went there, they established that there were some paramilitary groups who were terrorising the people, including the police, and that they were helpless. I believe that a different team went there to establish the facts. But I was telling you about the time that we were there. All the rest happened later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. As for this first visit to the four municipalities, as we'll call it, let me ask you this: Where did the traffic accident happen? Can you just tell me the location where it is. Don't tell me in detail about the accident.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: It was in Serbia. There's a cross-roads at the border. This was the only free road, the only passable road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about that later. Between these four municipalities, did you have to enter the Republic of Serbia in order to get there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. There was no other way. When we went to Foca, we went into two countries, practically. We travelled through Serbia and Montenegro. That was the only passable road. And it was the same for Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Between Bijeljina and Zvornik, did you have to pass through territory controlled by Muslim forces, that is, did you actually do this?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: The road between Bijeljina and Zvornik was free.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I mean when you're going towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, towards Bratunac, yes. Let me just explain. On the Zvornik-Bijeljina-Brcko road, you have -- it's practically one road; however, if you're going towards Skelani, you have to cross over to Serbia and travel along the other side of the Drina in order to finally get to Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Specifically I want to know whether you at any point risked travelling through territory controlled by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: That was when we were travelling from Sarajevo and Pale. It was on that road. That's the road towards Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, I meant --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: No, not between Brcko and Bijeljina. That was on our way there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I thought that towards Bratunac there was a road that you had to pass.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: That was on our way there. We hadn't even arrived. This was around Sarajevo and Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, if we're done with that visit, and we have already explained that you didn't write a report, according to what you said by way of introduction, the following visit, documented by a written report, was the one covered by the report on the activities of the police stations at Vogosca and Ilijas. It's under tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 00397, which is an exhibit, P989. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's turn to the last page of the report to see the signatures, and I'll come back to the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, can you identify your signature down there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the other person who went with you? It says here that it is Drago Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I can comment on this. Drago Borovcanin is mentioned under number 1, and I'm mentioned under number 2. When there are joint inspections or audits, the Police Administration is mentioned first and the Crime Prevention and Detection Department is mentioned second because the regular police are more numerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us turn to the first page, and I don't mean the cover page, and the section about the Vogosca SJB. Let us wait for the English translation. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this to jog your memory, and then I'll ask you about the contents of this report. Are you done?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Unless you have anything special to say about Vogosca, I would like to go to the fourth paragraph in Serbian, which begins with "It is necessary to point out."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is on the same page in the English version, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please read this paragraph. You don't have to read it aloud. Please explain what this is about. What personnel problems is Vogosca SJB faced with?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: There were problems with the chief of the station, the commander of the station, and all the executive personnel. This is more police business, but I know about it. There too, as far as I know, because we stayed there for a couple of hours, there was no chief of SJB. There was no commander either. They didn't have appointments. If I remember well then, Boro Maksimovic was there at the time. And Vlado Kelovic, I think. I didn't remember when I first mentioned it, but, yes, they had some kind of appointments. But the latter part was done by Drago Borovcanin because this had do with the uniform police, so it isn't my line of business. They had appointments -- or, rather, they didn't have appointments from the MUP - but did they actually have appointments? - I think there were appointments by the Crisis Staff, this Boro Maksimovic. I think he was wounded at the time. There may have been an attack on the police station by some group.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Were there any problems with the staffing of this police station bearing in mind what you've just said, that Maksimovic and the others were appointed by the local authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I know about this, but actually more from a later period because I worked for the Crime Prevention and Detection Administration. There was resistance there, resistance to the appointment of people whom we wanted, we the ministry. We wanted people from the service. We always relied on the people who had worked in the service before rather than on these upstarts, this party personnel, because they didn't have the adequate experience and knowledge. And the same problem was in Vogosca. And I know that this problem wasn't solved and it was transferred to the assistant minister. Dobro Planojevic told me about it. There was a problem with the people whom we had nominated, but there was also a problem with the uniformed police, whether they would get appointments where the local authorities had the say. Actually, they had more of a say than we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. And did the ministry then appointment people to these positions we're talking about, that is, chief and commander, and how was it implemented in the field? Were there any problems?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I cannot remember all details, but I know that the inspectors went there again after a month or so to solve the problem. I think Milanovic went there, maybe even Planojevic, to appoint our man. As far as crime is concerned, we nominated Zivko Lazarevic, who was a very good inspector; and we nominated Brano Vlaco, who used to work at the CSB. But I remember that we --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. The paragraph you are now talking about is on the following page. It's on this page in Serbian, but it's on the following page in English. That's why I interrupted you, to call up the following page. Here it is. Here in this paragraph these two names are mentioned in the centre of the page, Vlaco and the other. Are these the people you nominated?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, but when we were there and completed our job and returned, since we also had problems in getting there. So I don't want this to sound as if I'm complaining all the time. There were also sniper shots on our way there, so we went back on a different route. We nominated Zivko Lazarevic and Brano Vlaco, but it was upon the initiative of Milos Zuban maybe, I'm not sure, or Cedo Kljajic, or possibly Dobro was the one who suggested that we should nominate these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do read your proposal with all the names. Read them out but slowly, please. It's at the bottom of this page in Serbian. Please read it out aloud, just the names.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: "We suggest that the employee working there so far, Zivko Lazarevic, be appointed head."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: "And that Branislav Vlaco, inspector in the former Sarajevo CSB, be appointed crime prevention inspector." He was an economist by training and he worked on white collar crime, not general crime. That's why I know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the Vogosca SJB?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You stated his nickname or shortened first name; please state it again for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: It is Brano. I know the man personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, was your staffing proposal accepted or what was the outcome?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: There were problems there. I think that he left sometime -- at some point later and did something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know where he went and what he did?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. Now he's the manager of the Raiffeisen Bank in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the accused's microphone be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with Boro Maksimovic and Vlado Kelovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I think that Boro Maksimovic was wounded --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: At the beginning. But what happened finally? Did he stay?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: They were removed, but it was after the arrival of the other team. They were removed from their positions. They were people nominated by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know why they were removed? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, the reason was unprofessional conduct and the failure to take adequate measures from their job description that were necessary for the operation of the SJB, which is keeping up law and order, combatting crime, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the last page of this document and focus on the Ilijas SJB.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The microphone of the second accused is switched on again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have we found Ilijas in the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please focus on this second paragraph, halfway through. You were saying here that they have poor communications due to poor VHF channels. What was the communications system like at the stations you visited? Was it operational?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: At the beginning, in May, some lines were down at the local level. I'm not a communications guy, but we didn't really understand why it was like that because Vogosca and Ilijas were only some 20 kilometres apart, but they couldn't communicate, nonetheless. It may have been for reasons that have to do with the communications system. Possibly there was interference. Zvornik and Sarajevo couldn't communicate, but I understood that. I didn't understand why these two couldn't. The communications system was disrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you now about the eastern part that you visited before we move on to the west. To which CSB did the SJBs from the eastern part that you moved about in belong to before the war, organisationally speaking, at the time of the previous MUP? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Before the war, the ministry had eight centres, I believe: Bihac, Banja Luka, Doboj, Tuzla, Sarajevo, Gorazde, Mostar. Eight. Is that eight? Yes, eight. And these public security services or Security Services Centres had some SJBs under them that were organised at the municipal level. Tuzla included the following municipalities: Brcko, Bijeljina, Ugljevik, Zvornik, Vlasenica, Sekovic, Milici, Srebrenica, Gradacac. I think there was Srebrenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Here is my question: What about these municipalities that were left without their superior centre; how did they function at the beginning and what situation did you find there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: After our arrival and once we made a snap-shot, we saw that they weren't functioning. I'm talking about the management. The other stations such as Ugljevik, Bijeljina, Brcko, Zvornik, Bratunac - how should I put it? - in early 1992 they were left hanging. The organisation hadn't been up and running. The MUP hadn't been established yet. I know that later they were placed under Sarajevo CSB, such as Bratunac, Zvornik, Milici, Vlasenica, and at that time there were many problems until they were re-subordinated, as it were. Only local authorities had the say there, the Crisis Staffs and what have you. That's why our intention was to include them in the functioning of the ministry, legally speaking, and that they be included in our chain of command. There was a bigger rift because of that. We had no influence there, no influence on these stations. I'm talking about May, June, and July when I first went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you remember the Gorazde CSB of the once MUP and the stations that remained a part of the MUP of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: As far as I recall, and I'm more familiar with the Sarajevo Centre, I know about places in the Tuzla sector and after the war and I know that the Tuzla Centre included Rogatica, Visegrad, Rudo, Foca, and Cajnice. It practically was this territorial organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We'll have to correct something in the transcript. It says that the Tuzla Centre included these municipalities, but my question referred to Gorazde. You said that you were more familiar with the Tuzla region?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So what you just listed refers to the Gorazde CSB; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. What you said a moment ago regarding the stations from the Tuzla area, did it also apply to the Gorazde area? Can you tell us who controlled Gorazde throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same situation. It's logical that it would be the same situation. There were other problems. This was my view of things, and this may not be my field of expertise. There were problems regarding the organisation of the prosecutor's office and the courts. Nothing functioned properly in the areas that we visited. That was our understanding. Wherever we went we saw that the prosecutor's office or the courts were not functioning, so these stations and these municipalities were left as I put it a moment ago, hanging. They were nobody's. They were outside of our organisation, outside the area of both the judiciary and the police. The judiciary at the time was rather slow and inefficient. I believe that we were better than they were, in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. From the police point of view, did you find processed case files but they couldn't be handed over to anybody, they were just filed in drawers because there was nobody to hand them over to?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes. There were such cases, and there is a report. But it's impossible to remember everything because it's been a long time. I know that there were problems, particularly relating to the organisation of the judiciary and the prosecutor's office. I know about this because when we left Sarajevo, when our supervisors told us to go and look into things, we asked, Well, what do we look at? We were to look at the conditions. Somebody gave me a document that I carried with me, and it related to the organisation of the prosecutor's office and the judiciary. I believe this was some decisions. I can't remember whether it was the Presidency that made a decision forming courts, the prosecutor's office, and prisons. But since they were unable to send these to the field, it arrived to the administration, and then we were to carry this document with us. I remember that. However, the places that we visited, like Visegrad and Foca, Brcko, Rudo, Cajnice, the prosecuted's office wasn't functioning at all, and neither was the court. That was what we found. So the case files were just left there. And as for the civilian prosecutor's office, while it was being set up, the stations were supposed to keep functioning, and the case files that belonged to the military prosecutor's office were to be sent to Bileca. That was -- those were our instructions, as far as I recall. And it was a problem, I mean, as far as I remember, this wasn't organised at all at the time that I left the crime service.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Orasanin, I believe that based on the chronology of things we are now at your arrival to the CSB in Doboj. Do you agree with me that that was the next place you visited chronologically, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So according to the chronology, Doboj follows; right? Very well. I will first show you a document so we could establish when it was that you left. Just a moment, let me find it. There we go, it's tab 11. And this is Exhibit P404. Please take a look before I ask you a question. Mr. Orasanin, do you recall this authorisation?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it now. Initially I couldn't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you remember where you were when this authorisation was drafted and who drafted it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Having viewed this document, I remember that I was in Brcko. This document was written by Nikola Milanovic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: One moment. Who is Nikola Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: He is an inspector in the Crime Prevention Administration and he was with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please go on about the authorisation and its origins. Who wrote it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: We had already set off. I might have forgotten some things, but there were some problems about our presence, about us checking identity cards without any sort of authorisation. We weren't authorised to work there, and there were various checks along the way. So this authorisation was written in Brcko. He had contacted Goran Macar on the telephone and we laid down some tasks and obligations and also identity cards so that we could go there. That's why it has the stamp. It was in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. The document says "Authorisation," so that's what we'll call it. Please tell me who signed this authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I believe it was signed by Milanovic, I think. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milanovic ask authorisation from Goran Macar on the telephone to draft this authorisation and even to sign it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: He talked to him on the phone and he sought approval from Goran Macar. He sought approval from Goran Macar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you had this document with you when you set off for Doboj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now that you've seen the date at the top --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be the best course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milanovic -- Mr. Orasanin, I apologise, Mr. Orasanin, as you can see the date that the document bears, can you tell us how many days after that it was that you went to Doboj? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: We continued on our way the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And who met you and where did you first report?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: The rule is that when you arrive, you report to the supervisor, that is, the chief of the SJB, who at the time was Andrija Bjelosevic, and he met us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to talk to the chief of the SJB?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes. We had a coffee with him and we discussed the situation in his centre. And later we had a meeting with the chief of the crime service and continued with what our task was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you something because of Ms. Korner's objection. We have a correction to make to the transcript. I believe it was line 12 on page 71. Could you please repeat the function of Mr. Andrija Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: He was the chief of the Doboj CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now I can say that the mistake was that it was recorded that he was the chief of the SJB, but we've corrected it. And what did you discuss with Mr. Bjelosevic? Did you explain to him the purposes of your visit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: We discussed the situation regarding crime because we were a team that was authorised for crime prevention. Nikola Milanovic, myself, and Ostoja Minic were there from the Crime Service Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Did Mr. Bjelosevic brief you about the situation at the CSB in Doboj? And if you can recall, can you tell us what it was that he said?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: As far as I recall that short meeting with the chief, he told us about the situation regarding crime, especially about some murders. He told us that he had some problems with the relationship between the SJB and the CSB, the functions, and there was a similar problem in the territory of other centres, where the problems might have been a little milder than in the east. The SJBs exercised more authority than they should have. And as for the reserve police and the SJB in Doboj, I know that there were some later orders. And I was told to look into what was wrong about the reserve police, even though that wasn't our job, but there were some problems there. And I know that there were some requests made by the ministry. There was a problem, and the reserve police was to be reduced, the numbers were to be reduced, because there were some thousand reserve policemen, and Andrija told us about this. He said that Chief Petrovic, who was the chief of the SJB, wouldn't listen to him. So these were two problems: There were problems with crime and there were problems with the uniformed police, that is, with the reserve police. I know that there was an order later for the numbers to be reduced, but these were requests from the army. And as far as I recall, and I know that there were objections raised later on as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Bjelosevic speak to you about the organisational problems of the CSB? Did he speak about these problems?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, a man cannot remember everything. But I know roughly what the problems were. To my mind, he couldn't exert any influence on the work of the SJBs that belonged to his centre. He complained about - was it Modrica or Samac or Derventa? - anyway, some stations belonging to his centre. The station chiefs, to my mind, had more power than he did. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did he speak about military matters and how these things affected the work of the centre?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: As for the relationship between the police and the military, there were special problems, especially organisational problems, at the centre. I know the minister's orders. And somebody told me when we set off from the MUP - was it Goran Macar? I don't know - anyway, take a look into that. Apart from the crime and the murders and all that, take a look at the relations between the SJBs and the CSB, and that was because of the downsizing order. And the military had objections against the police organising itself in such a massive scale and due to combat readiness, and this is the source of the conflict between the MUP and the army. They wanted some of these men to be re-subordinated to the military. They were arguing that this was a brigade that wasn't really -- that the MUP didn't really need, or anybody else, so that they should be put at the disposal of the military. It wasn't done then, but I know that other teams went there later. And this man Petrovic, the station chief, didn't do it again, again failed to do it. So the stations were really very powerful. But I cannot remember now if Petrovic was -- because we always contacted people from the service and not so much with those who were not from the service. And as far as I know, we didn't really contact Petrovic at all. Yes, we did, actually, when it comes to the Crime Prevention Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When you say you contacted people from the service, who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I mean the professionals who worked for the service before and who were not newly appointed and for the simple reason that I didn't like them, whoever had appointed them because they weren't professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Petrovic belong to this second group of those who were not professionals?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What happened after the meeting with Mr. Bjelosevic? How did you continue?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: We only had a short meeting with him. And then, in line with our instructions, we had a meeting with the chief of the Crime Prevention Service, whose name is Vojo Blagojevic, I think. And then we inspected some files. We were only interested in serious crimes and whether they were registered, what the procedure -- what procedure was applied, were they entered in the relevant log-book, what activities were taken. And we demanded that operative groups be set up, but they were also short of operatives and inspectors. And we insisted that this be dealt with, that the prosecutor's office must receive all criminal reports, and that this should be tackled. I know that there were some 10 or 11 murders, and that was actually the subject of our meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you invite anybody from the judiciary to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: It was our initiative. When the three of us arrived, it was some sort of a rule that first you go to the police and then you have a meeting with them; then you go to the prosecutor's office, if there is one, and the court. And we are always careful to leave the initiative to the prosecutor's office and the court first and then to the police, because they should be the first to act, the prosecutors. And then we had a meeting with the representative of the court whose name was Sinisa Djordjevic. He was a lawyer. I don't know which prosecutor was present. And they especially pointed out the problem of co-operation and, as far as I remember, the presence of the accused, that is, providing security for him, and securing evidence or investigative activities. These are the problems that we discussed. And with that investigative activities, of course, there can be no results or a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just tell us about the problem with the accused. I think it wasn't recorded properly. What was the problem with the accused? Could you define it in one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't do it in one sentence because we in the police don't use the term "accused." I said that it was the meeting with the court president. We discussed it together, and they pointed out that they had problems, and these are their problems, with securing the accused for the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When you say securing, you mean making sure that he's present?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I mean, making sure that he's present, that he's brought in, and all other investigative measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I only intervened because it was recorded differently. Mr. Orasanin, let us focus on something else, if there's time. You said that -- or, rather, you mentioned the files about this most serious crimes. What kind of crimes were those and what about those files?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Our first -- when we first went there, we spoke to the chief of the Crime Prevention Service and he briefed us about some cases and crime reports that were pending, and -- because we wanted to see whether they were doing anything. We insisted that these be submitted to the prosecutor's office. That was the basic thing. And that something be done to follow them up. We only wanted that they should do what they were supposed to, only what follows from our rules and instructions. And he briefed us on these murders. And as far as I remember there was also some white collar crime and there was also some violent crime, some 10 or 11 cases, I think. There were a couple of murders with known perpetrators, and these criminal reports were immediately submitted. But there were also cases with unknown perpetrators. Then we wanted them to draft operative plans and assign these tasks to some people. That was our role.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Can you remember the structure of the victims from these most serious crimes, I mean violent crimes and murders?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I may be slightly off the mark but most victims were Bosniaks. Six, 7, there were a couple of Serbs maybe and one Croatia victim. And when it comes to unknown perpetrators, there were some 9 or 10 or so. I can't remember exactly. And that was key because evidence had to be collected for those cases with unknown perpetrators and then for those files to be submitted to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Were there any cases that had been submitted with prosecutor's office before your arrival, and I mean the most serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there may have been one criminal report against a known perpetrator and maybe some criminal reports against unknown perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And about those that were pending, you mentioned the setting up of some groups. How did you assign the tasks? That's what I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: I must say that we weren't duty-bound to do that. We were just inspecting. It was up to the chief of the Crime Prevention Service because he was the operative. We didn't have our own operatives there; we were from the centre. And he was tasked to set up groups consisting of operatives and forensic technicians to work on the detection of these crimes and their perpetrators. And of course it is a legal obligation for the criminal report to be submitted to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: On page 77, I believe it's line 16, it was recorded 74 operatives; did you mention any such number?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, did you have any own operatives that could have taken over that job?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: No, no way. 74 operatives? We didn't have as many in the whole administration, I think. We have just seen how many operatives there were in the Crime Prevention and Detection Service. But if we were to take all the operatives from the Banja Luka, Doboj, and Trebinje Centres and put them together, we wouldn't have more than 50, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I just wanted to correct the transcript. I didn't want to dwell on this. Mr. Orasanin, do you know whether these tasks that you assigned to the chief of the administration with the centre were followed up after your departure?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, another team went there later. They visited the Doboj Centre again. And as far as I know, the criminal reports were submitted to the prosecutor's office. Of course, I wouldn't know how much work had to be done to achieve that, but I know that the prosecutor's office did receive criminal reports. This has to do with the instruction on the combatting of crime that we had taken over earlier, so it was an obligation. I'm not saying that we contrived anything. It was just a procedure. And it's a fact that these criminal reports were submitted to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, why is it important that a criminal report is submitted to the prosecutor's office even against an unknown perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: According to the instructions. And we are also duty-bound to do so. I believe that any police in the world does it that way. When a criminal offence is registered in the log-book, which is kept at the police station, then an on-site investigation is made by the investigative magistrate and a prosecutor, they conduct some activities, and the police and the crime enforcement service are there as assistants, and everybody does that part of the work. In order to shed light on the offence, we must proceed in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure. One of them is conducting an on-site investigation, forensic activities, searches, interviews. However, the law was different at the time. The Law on Criminal Procedure had a provision allowing the investigative magistrate to transfer his work to the police, but that only applied in case of lesser crimes. In case of more serious crimes, the investigative magistrate and the prosecutor had to be present. And the police only provided assistance as ordered by the person in charge of the on-site investigation. So the investigative magistrate and the prosecutor play a much more important role than we.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you one more question before the end. Does this anything have to do with the securing of evidence in relation to reports against unknown perpetrators? Why do you have to report to the prosecutor? Does that have to do with the securing of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If we know what the investigative actions are and know what special investigative actions are, they cannot be undertaken without an order. That's how it was before. As for how it is now, the prosecutor has more powers, as far as I know. That's how things are at the moment. So the organs of the interior do not do anything without the presence of the prosecutor. And then we did things as we had before the war. We were able to conduct things with verbal approval for minor crimes. And that's why between 1992, and which is important, we were handicapped. If the prosecutor's office or the court were not present, then the hands of the police were tied. You could register a crime and keep the file in a drawer. That was the case in Foca, for example. We gave an order for an on-site investigation; however, there was nobody present at the court. I might have given a long explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I note the time, and I would like to move on to specific cases, which inspectors from the administration looked at in Doboj. That's a new topic, so it might be good for us to break a little earlier today and continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I try one last time about leading questions. A question such as "does this have anything to do with securing of evidence in relation to reports against unknown perpetrators, why do you have to report to the prosecutor, does that have anything to do with the securing of evidence?" That is a leading question. The proper question was the one sentence in the middle, "why do you have to report to the prosecutor?" Anything else suggests the answer that you want. And of course, the upshot is that it devalues the evidence your own witness gives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So Mr. Cvijetic has again been reminded. Thank you. Mr. Orasanin, we're about to take the adjournment for the day. I am to remind you that having been sworn as a witness, you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side until you are released by the Chamber. Moreover, in such conversations as you may have with anybody else, you cannot discuss your testimony. Do you understand what I've just said? So we take the adjournment to resume -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We take the adjournment until tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of June, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
